cases.title: Third Jiangxi Highway: 747 households rebuilt their houses for the Ganzhou-Ruijin expressway
cases.place: Ruijin-Ganzhou expressway corridor, Ganzhou prefecture, Jiangxi, China
cases.point: Approximate. The coordinates sit on Yudu county town, about halfway along the corridor. The expressway runs 117 km from Ganzhou to Ruijin in southern Jiangxi, and the completion report counts 66 villages affected by land acquisition along it. The project also paid for local roads in Ganzhou prefecture.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Third Jiangxi Highway Project, P093906. Loan IBRD-48300 of US$200 million, approved 27 June 2006, with the loan and project agreements conformed on 23 November 2006, effective 8 February 2007 and closed 31 December 2010. US$189.7 million was disbursed. US$5 million was cancelled after the Bank declared misprocurement on a local road contract.

cases.conditions: The project was classified Category A for environmental assessment and triggered the Bank's policy on involuntary resettlement (OP 4.12). A resettlement action plan and a resettlement policy framework were prepared in November 2005 and disclosed before appraisal, which the Bank carried out in April 2006. The completion report's annex says the plan estimated 7,826 people and 1,714 households affected by land acquisition and resettlement and 274,370 square metres of housing to be demolished.

companies.name: Jiangxi Provincial Transport Department (JPTD)
companies.role: Implementing agency for the expressway, working through a Provincial Resettlement Office
companies.desc: The provincial roads authority in Jiangxi, in south-eastern China. It ran the expressway works and the resettlement under this loan through a provincial resettlement office. The Bank's completion report records no activity for it outside the project.

companies.name: Ganzhou City Prefecture (GCP)
companies.role: Implementing agency for the local roads component
companies.desc: The prefecture-level government for southern Jiangxi. It ran the local roads part of the loan. The Independent Evaluation Group cut its performance rating after it awarded one road contract outside Bank rules.

cases.community: The completion report sets the resettlement plan and the outcome side by side. Against the plan, 853.3 hectares of land were acquired rather than 835.7, including 348.6 hectares of farmland rather than 303.7; 214,842 square metres of housing were demolished rather than 274,370; 66 villages were affected rather than 63; and 1,652 households and 7,599 people were affected by land acquisition and resettlement, against 1,714 households and 7,826 people planned. Compensation came to US$30.14 million against US$26.88 million planned. The borrower's own completion report, annexed to the Bank's, gives the house moves. Resettlement on the expressway was formally launched at a meeting in Ganzhou on 16 August 2006, before the loan became effective in February 2007. By the end of December 2007 house relocation "had basically been completed", and among 747 households who had to relocate their houses, 606 had rebuilt, 142 were still building and one had not rebuilt. The last three unrelocated houses were moved by the end of January 2009 after compensation agreements were reached. Compensation was paid into individual bank accounts. The Bank's own annex says approximately 200 complaints were received and handled during the resettlement stage and that no intractable conflicts arose. It names one resettlement site, the concentrated resettlement area at Maoping village, Luo'ao town, Yudu county, and records the relocation of Qiantang Primary School. Surveys by the Center for Involuntary Resettlement Research at Wuhan University reported that average living area per household rose 17 per cent and the share of brick and concrete houses rose 38 per cent.
cases.outcome: The resettlement is recorded as compliant. The completion report of 29 June 2011 rates the project outcome Satisfactory, Bank performance Satisfactory, borrower performance Highly Satisfactory and risk to the development outcome Low or Negligible. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 10 September 2012 agrees on outcome and Bank performance but cuts borrower performance to Satisfactory, because Ganzhou City Prefecture awarded a contract for a local road outside Bank guidelines, which led the Bank to declare misprocurement and cancel US$5 million of the loan, and because the prefecture was erratic in submitting and replacing candidate roads. The Group says land acquisition and resettlement were carried out without major issues and that compensation was paid in a timely manner.
cases.displaced_label: households that had to relocate their houses on the Ruijin-Ganzhou expressway, as counted in the borrower's completion report annexed to the Bank's report
cases.displaced_note: The figure of 747 households is the borrower's count, in the Jiangxi Provincial Transport Department's completion report annexed to the Bank's completion report, of households that had to relocate their houses on the Ruijin-Ganzhou expressway. The Bank's own annex counts 1,652 households and 7,599 people affected by land acquisition and resettlement, and 214,842 square metres of housing demolished; neither of those is a count of people moved. The Bank does not give a project-wide count of households relocated. ICIJ puts displacement for this project at 10,611 and lists it in its confirmed-displacement table. No figure in the Bank's documents opened matches 10,611. ICIJ's own method page states what its figures count. It looked for what the Bank's documents call "Project-Affected People (PAP)" or "displaced people", searching those documents for the words "affected", "PAP" or "displaced". Where a document counted only households, it says it was necessary to look up the average number of family members per household. Because the documents do not all separate temporary impacts from permanent ones, it "decided to include all impacts". Its data stops at 31 December 2014. The documents do not explain how ICIJ arrived at its figure.

cases.confidence_note: The core harm rests on one body of evidence. The World Bank's own documents are the only source found: the completion report, written by Bank staff with a borrower section annexed, and the Independent Evaluation Group's validation of that report. Those findings are the lender reporting on its own project. No press report, NGO field study, court record or Inspection Panel complaint about this resettlement was found. Searches in Chinese, including for the project corridor and for named places in it, returned only World Bank documents and local government notices. The 747-household figure is the borrower's own report on its own resettlement, printed in an annex to the lender's report.
cases.ecosystem: The completion report's annex describes the mitigation work: slopes rehabilitated with grass, trees and shrubs, sprinkler systems to hold down construction dust, and a ban on discharging untreated wastewater from the 12 construction camps into rivers or reservoirs, with fines attached. The Independent Evaluation Group records that the environmental assessment and management plan were reviewed at appraisal and found satisfactory.

lvwhy.project: A World Bank investment loan paid for the expressway and the local roads that required the land and the houses.
lvwhy.land: 853.3 hectares were acquired, including 348.6 hectares of farmland, and 214,842 square metres of housing were demolished.

cases.whole: The loan paid for 117 km of the Ruijin-Ganzhou Expressway, completed and opened to traffic in March 2009 ahead of schedule, and for a local roads improvement programme in Ganzhou prefecture, which accounted for about five per cent of the loan. The expressway part was built fast and the loan disbursed faster than planned. The local roads part went badly: the Bank declared misprocurement on the Chongyi-Longgou road contract and cancelled US$5 million, the prefecture changed the candidate roads repeatedly, and the programme's scope was cut at restructuring. All the figures are the Bank's own and the borrower's own. No independent check was found.

cases.title: Trung Son dam: 695 households moved in Thanh Hoa, 17 per cent of them away from the planned sites
cases.place: Trung Son commune, Quan Hoa district, Thanh Hoa, Viet Nam, with resettlement sites in Quan Hoa, Muong Lat and Van Ho districts
cases.point: Approximate. The coordinates sit on the dam site on the Ma River in Trung Son commune, Quan Hoa district, Thanh Hoa province. The reservoir, the access road, the resettlement sites and the transmission lines are spread across three provinces; the completion report puts the 695 relocated households at 13 resettlement points on four sites in Quan Hoa and Muong Lat districts of Thanh Hoa and Van Ho district of Son La.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: VN-Trung Son Hydropower Project, P084773. Loan IBRD-80410 of SDR 241.21 million, US$330 million equivalent, approved 26 April 2011, signed in June 2011, effective 23 September 2011, closing extended from 31 December 2017 to 31 December 2019. US$291.12 million was disbursed. The borrower put in a further US$64.42 million, against US$81.72 million planned.

cases.conditions: The project was Environmental Category A and triggered eight safeguard policies: environmental assessment, natural habitats, pest management, physical cultural resources, involuntary resettlement, indigenous peoples, safety of dams and projects on international waterways. A Resettlement, Livelihoods and Ethnic Minorities Development Plan was prepared from 2008 and revised through 2013, with a separate resettlement policy framework for the transmission line. A first restructuring on 30 December 2015 let the loan pay for houses built by the households themselves, after consultation in which 88.5 per cent of displaced households said they preferred cash to houses built by the project company. A second restructuring in December 2018 extended the closing date to upgrade the access road and resettlement infrastructure, which the Bank says had been degraded by the end of implementation and damaged by heavy rain and floods, and to deal with dam safety risks from large landslides.

companies.name: Trung Son Hydropower Company Limited (TSHPCo)
companies.role: Project company; carried out compensation, resettlement and the livelihood programme
companies.desc: A company set up under Vietnam Electricity, the state power utility, to build and run the Trung Son plant. It paid the compensation, built the resettlement sites and ran the grievance system described in the Bank's reports.

companies.name: Vietnam Electricity (EVN)
companies.role: State power utility, parent of the project company
companies.desc: Vietnam's state-owned electricity company. The Bank's reports say practices from this project were later taken up by EVN on other hydropower projects.

cases.community: The completion report says the project affected 3,413 households, of which 695 had to be relocated, and that the project affected approximately 10,600 people, 3,413 households, directly or indirectly. The 695 households moved to 13 resettlement points at four sites in Quan Hoa, Muong Lat and Van Ho districts. Of those households, 83 per cent moved to the resettlement areas and 17 per cent did not, the report saying they preferred other locations. Each relocated household received 400 square metres of residential land and 300 square metres of garden land. The project built 4.5 per cent of the relocation houses and the households built 95.5 per cent with project money. A further 47 resettlement plots were arranged for households affected by the West Thanh Hoa road. The report counts 468 households losing more than 10 per cent of their productive land, and 46 affected villages taking part in a livelihood restoration programme with a budget of VND 22.6 billion, about US$971,165. On compensation the report's text and its own table do not agree: the text says total compensation of VND 541.3 billion, US$24.98 million, had been paid by closing, while table 5 totals VND 581,250 million for the same US$24,977,438. The communities are mainly Thai, Muong and H'mong, and consultations were held in those languages. A separate Bank report of September 2020 names two villages that refused the site chosen for them: people of Ta Lao village in Tan Xuan commune said the planned site at An village was 20 km away, particularly hot, sheltered in a valley and short of water, and would have meant travelling over 20 km of hilly roads to reach their fields; villagers from Ta Ban also asked for an alternative. After seven meetings with Ta Lao and ten with Ta Ban, the company let the communities pick their own site. In a final evaluation in 2018, 82.2 per cent of surveyed households said they were satisfied with how complaints were handled.
cases.killed_note: The completion report says that resettlement sites were hit by heavy rain and floods during the Bebinca storm of July and August 2018, which produced the highest inflows ever recorded at the dam, damaged access roads, electricity, water supply and schools at resettlement sites, and that it was reported one person died as a result of the storm and six houses collapsed. The report attributes this to the storm, which it treats as outside the control of the government and the implementing agencies, and it is not counted here as a death caused by the project. The company repaired the collapsed houses and the infrastructure from project funds.
cases.outcome: The resettlement is recorded as compliant and the project is rated at the top of the scale. The completion report of 24 June 2020 rates the outcome Highly Satisfactory, Bank performance Highly Satisfactory and the quality of monitoring Substantial. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 30 September 2020 agrees with all three and adds Substantial for the quality of the report, recording no disagreement. The Group states that all eight safeguard policies triggered were complied with, and also states, of the same document, that the completion report "does not specifically confirm whether or not the above policies were complied with" for the environmental safeguards. It says 1,885 hectares of land were affected across three provinces. Separately, the Bank's Integrity Vice Presidency published a redacted report in November 2018 on a consultancy contract of about US$10 million under this project: it found that the firm it calls Company X misrepresented the availability of its proposed team leader and the qualifications and availability of its proposed deputy team leader, leaving the project and the implementing agency without a full-time international deputy team leader for about ten months. That finding concerns a contract, not the resettlement.
cases.displaced_label: households relocated by the dam, the reservoir and the associated works (World Bank completion report)
cases.displaced_note: The World Bank's completion report counts 695 households relocated out of 3,413 households affected, and says the project affected approximately 10,600 people, 3,413 households, directly or indirectly. It gives no total number of people in the 695 relocated households. ICIJ puts displacement for this project at 10,591 and lists it in its confirmed-displacement table; that is close to the completion report's figure for people affected directly or indirectly, not to the number relocated. ICIJ's own method page states what its figures count. It looked for what the Bank's documents call "Project-Affected People (PAP)" or "displaced people", searching those documents for the words "affected", "PAP" or "displaced". Where a document counted only households, it says it was necessary to look up the average number of family members per household. Because the documents do not all separate temporary impacts from permanent ones, it "decided to include all impacts". Its data stops at 31 December 2014. The documents do not explain how ICIJ arrived at its figure.

cases.confidence_note: The core harm rests on one body of evidence. Every figure here comes from the World Bank or from the project company reporting through it: the completion report, the Independent Evaluation Group's validation, the Bank's own 2020 report on the project's social management, and the Bank's integrity report. The lender is reporting on its own project, and the satisfaction figures come from surveys commissioned by the project. Searches in Vietnamese, including for resettlement in Quan Hoa and Muong Lat and for complaints about compensation at the dam, returned no press report, NGO field study, court record or Inspection Panel complaint about this resettlement.
cases.ecosystem: The reservoir flooded land on the Ma River in a mountainous area of northern Thanh Hoa. The project ran studies of aquatic and terrestrial biodiversity, a reservoir vegetation clearance plan, a reservoir hydrodynamic and water quality model and an assessment of impacts on fish, and produced six wildlife monitoring reports and 15 fish monitoring reports. The Independent Evaluation Group says seven of the ten environmental triggers it recorded were rated Satisfactory and three Moderately Satisfactory, with minor shortcomings in housekeeping, waste management and occupational health and safety at work sites and construction camps, and some gaps in site restoration at quarries, camps and workshops measured against international best practice. Intense rainfall in August 2018 made the right bank downstream of the dam slide during a long spillway discharge, and tension cracks appeared in the cut slope upstream in August and November 2018.

lvwhy.project: A World Bank loan of US$330 million paid for the dam, the reservoir, the access road, the transmission lines and the resettlement programme.
lvwhy.land: 1,885 hectares were affected across three provinces, and 695 households lost their houses to the reservoir and the works.
lvwhy.finance: The loan was restructured in 2015 so that Bank money could pay households to build their own replacement houses.

cases.whole: The loan paid for a 260 MW hydropower plant on the Ma River, its access road, resettlement sites, transmission lines and a substation, together with a livelihoods programme for 46 affected villages. Power output was slightly above target in 2017 and 2018 and fell in 2019 during a drought. The Bank reports the plant as meeting 8 of 10 criteria of the Hydropower Sustainability Protocol, and the project electrified about 800 households in the resettlement areas and affected villages. It reports the share of poor households in the project area falling from 23.8 per cent before the project to 16.8 per cent at completion, and 97 per cent of households with electricity. Reservoir impoundment was delayed by two to three months. Total project cost was US$355.4 million against US$411.7 million estimated. All the figures are the Bank's own or the project company's. No independent check was found.

cases.title: Ningxia highway: compensation delayed after the Bank and the province did not agree on rates
cases.place: Guyaozi-Qingtongxia expressway and National Highway 211, Lingwu, Wuzhong and Qingtongxia, Ningxia, China
cases.point: Approximate. The coordinates sit on Lingwu city, in the middle of the corridor. The expressway runs 75.68 km from Guyaozi through Lingwu and Wuzhong to Qingtongxia; the project also rehabilitated 65 km of National Highway 211 between Lingwu and Jiajiajuan and improved local roads elsewhere in Ningxia.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Ningxia Highway Project, P096920. Loan IBRD-78800 of US$250 million, approved 13 May 2010, with the loan agreement conformed on 22 July 2010, effective 27 October 2010 against a planned 27 August 2010, and closed 30 June 2015. The whole US$250 million was disbursed. Part of the civil works was financed retroactively and had begun about eight months before the launch mission of August 2010.

cases.conditions: The project was Category A for environmental assessment and triggered the Bank's policies on involuntary resettlement and natural habitats. A resettlement action plan and a policy framework were prepared in 2009 and 2010 and disclosed, and a resettlement information booklet setting out compensation rates, entitlements and grievance procedures was distributed to affected people on 10 July 2009. The Independent Evaluation Group records that the appraisal survey expected the expressway to affect 32 villages in 10 towns or townships, to require 575 hectares of permanent land acquisition including 297 hectares of irrigated farmland, to affect 2,395 households and 10,436 people from 32 villages through permanent land acquisition, to demolish 59,695 square metres of housing and to relocate 1,429 people in 310 households.

companies.name: Ningxia Transport Department (NTD)
companies.role: Executing agency; set up resettlement coordination offices in the affected cities
companies.desc: The transport authority of the Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region in north-west China. It ran this loan through a project management office and had previously run the Bank's Tri-Provincial Highway Project.

companies.name: Ningxia Highway Construction and Administration Bureau (NHCAB)
companies.role: Implementing body for the expressway and the national highway
companies.desc: The regional highway construction and administration bureau. With the transport department it set up resettlement coordination offices and assigned staff to affected villages along each expressway segment.

cases.community: The Independent Evaluation Group names two significant shortcomings in how the project was prepared, one of them about compensation: the preparation team did not adequately address social safeguards associated with resettlement compensation, because the Bank and the project management unit differed over fair compensation rates for affected households, and the absence of agreement on rates before approval "contributed to delays in payment of compensation during implementation". The Group says the supervision team took corrective action on those delays, and that the region later told it the affected people have now been compensated, with non-monetary compensation on top of the money, including 24 rural roads built for the villages and skills training. The completion report says compensation rates in Ningxia were relatively low, that the project added supporting measures endorsed by the transport department and the mayors of the affected cities, and that it mobilised extra funding for low-income households, including RMB 18,000 per household in Qingtongxia. It records moderate difficulties and delays in providing infrastructure for resettled households: land acquisition and house demolition were completed in 2013 and water and sewer services to relocated households were restored in 2014. It lists unfair or unreasonable compensation among the safeguard problems resolved during implementation, and says there were different interests among those to be resettled, those whose land holdings were significantly reduced and vulnerable people who were old or on low incomes, and that no complaints were filed. One existing weigh station on National Highway 211 was moved in 2014 to Huianpu. The Bank's documents name no affected village.
cases.outcome: The completion report of 8 December 2015 rates the outcome Satisfactory, Bank performance Satisfactory, borrower performance Satisfactory and risk to the development outcome Negligible to Low. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 29 July 2016 agrees on those ratings, recording no disagreement, although its table prints the completion report's risk rating as Negligible rather than Negligible to Low. The Group rates the quality of the completion report Modest. It writes that the report "does not provide sufficient information on the achievement of project objectives", that "there is too much non-objective assertion in most dimensions of the project and there is no convincing data/information on safeguard compliance", and that because land acquisition and resettlement were substantial, "there is very little information in the ICR on the actual numbers who were compensated in relation to the numbers identified at appraisal". On the resettlement itself it states that the report "provides no evidence on the actual number of people who were compensated as compared to the number identified at appraisal and provides no evidence whether the funding provided was adequate", and that the report's assertion that there were no negative environmental impacts and no issues with natural habitats is made without evidence.
cases.displaced_note: No count of how many people or households were actually moved appears in the Bank's documents opened for this project. The only relocation figures are from the appraisal survey, reported by the Independent Evaluation Group: 1,429 people in 310 households were to be relocated, and 2,395 households and 10,436 people in 32 villages were expected to be affected by permanent land acquisition. The completion report says land acquisition and house demolition were completed in 2013 and that water and sewer services to relocated households were restored in 2014, but it counts nobody. The Independent Evaluation Group says the report gives no evidence of the actual numbers compensated. ICIJ puts displacement for this project at 10,436 and lists it in its confirmed-displacement table; that is, to the person, the appraisal estimate of people affected by permanent land acquisition. ICIJ's own method page states what its figures count. It looked for what the Bank's documents call "Project-Affected People (PAP)" or "displaced people", searching those documents for the words "affected", "PAP" or "displaced". Where a document counted only households, it says it was necessary to look up the average number of family members per household. Because the documents do not all separate temporary impacts from permanent ones, it "decided to include all impacts". Its data stops at 31 December 2014. The documents do not explain how ICIJ arrived at its figure.

cases.confidence_note: The core harm rests on one body of evidence. The World Bank's own documents are the only source found: the completion report, written by Bank staff with a borrower section annexed, and the Independent Evaluation Group's validation of that report. Those findings are the lender reporting on its own project. No press report, NGO field study, court record or Inspection Panel complaint about this resettlement was found. Searches in Chinese, including for the project corridor and for named places in it, returned only World Bank documents and local government notices. The documented harm here is the delay in paying compensation, which is stated by the Bank's own evaluators rather than by anyone affected. How many people were moved, and how late the money was, are not in the record.
cases.ecosystem: A segment of the expressway crossed the experimental zone of the Baijitan National Nature Reserve, a vulnerable steppe ecosystem, and the road crosses the Yellow River on an extra-long bridge. Appraisal identified risks of soil erosion and disturbance to ecological and irrigation systems. The completion report says mitigation avoided negative impacts and that performance in the Baijitan segment was excellent; the Independent Evaluation Group says that assertion is made without supporting evidence. Pavement cracking appeared on both the expressway and National Highway 211 after the two-year defect liability period, and the province resurfaced at its own expense.

lvwhy.project: A World Bank loan of US$250 million paid for the expressway, the national highway rehabilitation and the local roads that required the land.
lvwhy.land: Appraisal expected 575 hectares of permanent land acquisition, including 297 hectares of irrigated farmland, affecting 2,395 households in 32 villages.

cases.whole: The loan paid for 75.68 km of four-lane expressway between Guyaozi and Qingtongxia, rehabilitation of about 65 km of National Highway 211, a local roads improvement programme, and three technical assistance studies on traffic safety, logistics and road maintenance. The first expressway segment opened in November 2011 and the rest a year later, apart from 3 km next to the Qingtongxia railway. Traffic on the expressway at opening was below forecast; on the local roads and the national highway it was above. A social impact survey of 134 households in 16 villages along 14 rural roads reported the number of people in poverty in seven villages falling 33 per cent, from 3,859 to 2,580, and average annual income per head rising 41 per cent, from RMB 3,464 to RMB 4,873. An assessment of the local roads programme's social impact was due under the loan covenants by December 2014 and was carried out only at closing in 2015, without baselines other than travel times and traffic volumes. All the figures are the Bank's own. No independent check was found.

cases.title: Zhejiang Urban Environment: 4,628 people lost houses across Ningbo, Hangzhou and Shaoxing
cases.place: Ningbo, Hangzhou and Shaoxing, Zhejiang, China
cases.point: Approximate. The coordinates sit on Ningbo, where five of the eight sub-projects with resettlement were. The others were the expansion of the Tianziling landfill in Hangzhou and two sub-projects in Shaoxing, the historic city-centre works and the Yue Kingdom conservation area.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Zhejiang Urban Environment Project, P066955. Loan IBRD-47240 of US$133 million, approved 29 January 2004, with the loan agreement conformed on 2 June 2004, effective 1 November 2004, closing extended from 30 June 2010 to 30 June 2011. US$132.6 million was disbursed. The loan was restructured twice, in 2008 and 2009, to use loan savings on two new components.

cases.conditions: The project was Category A for environmental assessment and triggered the Bank's policies on involuntary resettlement and on cultural property. Eight resettlement action plans were prepared, one for each sub-project with resettlement; six were completed between March and May 2003 and the remaining two in June 2006 and December 2008. Appraisal rated the risk that delays in land acquisition and resettlement could hold up the project as substantial.

companies.name: Zhejiang provincial and municipal project management offices
companies.role: Implementing agencies for the eight sub-projects with resettlement
companies.desc: Project offices at provincial level and in Ningbo, Hangzhou and Shaoxing, which ran the works and the land acquisition under this loan and submitted annual progress reports to the Bank.

companies.name: Hohai University and Eastern China Hydropower Design Institute
companies.desc: The university and design institute engaged to monitor the resettlement from outside the project offices and report to the Bank. Their assessments are the basis for the Bank's statements that living standards improved.

cases.community: The completion report's resettlement annex gives the outcome for the eight sub-projects: 141.92 hectares of land permanently acquired, 21.22 hectares used temporarily, and 161,064 square metres of housing and shop premises demolished, of which 111,544 square metres were housing and 49,520 square metres shops and enterprises. The total population affected was 7,025 people, of whom 4,628 were affected by house demolition and 2,397 by land use. Against the plan, the report shows 9,610 people expected to be affected through residential housing and 4,628 actually affected, and 247,564 square metres of demolition planned against 161,064 carried out. The affected people are counted by sub-project: 520 at Jiangdongnan in Ningbo, 60 at Zhenhai, 482 at Jiangnan, 1,789 at Cicheng, 621 at Dongqian Lake, 1,176 at the Tianziling landfill expansion in Hangzhou, 1,624 on the Shaoxing infrastructure works and 753 in the Yue Kingdom conservation area. Land acquisition and resettlement cost RMB 1,116 million, against RMB 910.34 million planned, which the Independent Evaluation Group puts at US$180 million against US$148.4 million. At the Jiangnan wastewater plant in Ningbo, the report says the higher cost was because land acquisition and resettlement were applied to all households within 500 metres of the plant boundary rather than 300 metres as planned at appraisal. In Shaoxing the higher cost was due to much higher compensation costs claimed by affected people during implementation. At Cicheng and Zhenhai and around Dongqian Lake the cost fell, because the scope was cut and because sewer and road routes were changed to reduce the number of people affected; the cultural heritage component was itself scaled down because of resettlement difficulties and high costs. The report says all affected people were resettled according to the plans, that compensation standards were at least those in the plans, that all compensation was paid on time and that all affected people were consulted throughout. No village or neighbourhood is named as a resettlement site.
cases.outcome: The resettlement is recorded as compliant. The completion report of 26 December 2011 rates the outcome Satisfactory, Bank performance Satisfactory, borrower performance Satisfactory and risk to the development outcome Modest. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 1 May 2014 cuts the outcome to Moderately Satisfactory, because it rates efficiency modest in the absence of sufficient evidence or benchmarks for the claims of cost-effectiveness, and cuts Bank performance to Moderately Satisfactory, citing the two years taken over project design and the added complexity from restructuring. It keeps borrower performance at Satisfactory. Its ratings table prints the risk to the development outcome as Moderate, for itself and for the completion report, where the completion report's own summary gives Modest.
cases.displaced_label: people affected by house demolition, out of 7,025 project-affected people (World Bank completion report)
cases.displaced_note: The World Bank's completion report counts 7,025 people affected across the eight sub-projects with resettlement, of whom 4,628 were affected by house demolition and 2,397 by land use, with 161,064 square metres of housing and shop premises demolished. The comparison table in the same annex puts the number planned to be affected through residential housing at 9,610 against 4,628 actually affected. The report gives no separate count of households moved. ICIJ puts displacement for this project at 10,251 and lists it in its confirmed-displacement table. No figure in the Bank's documents opened matches 10,251. ICIJ's own method page states what its figures count. It looked for what the Bank's documents call "Project-Affected People (PAP)" or "displaced people", searching those documents for the words "affected", "PAP" or "displaced". Where a document counted only households, it says it was necessary to look up the average number of family members per household. Because the documents do not all separate temporary impacts from permanent ones, it "decided to include all impacts". Its data stops at 31 December 2014. The documents do not explain how ICIJ arrived at its figure.

sources.title: About Evicted and Abandoned: methodology

cases.confidence_note: The core harm rests on one body of evidence. The World Bank's own documents are the only source found: the completion report, written by Bank staff with a borrower section annexed, and the Independent Evaluation Group's validation of that report. Those findings are the lender reporting on its own project. No press report, NGO field study, court record or Inspection Panel complaint about this resettlement was found. Searches in Chinese, including for the project corridor and for named places in it, returned only World Bank documents and local government notices.
cases.ecosystem: The project built sewerage and wastewater treatment in Ningbo, cleaned up Dongqian Lake and expanded the Tianziling landfill in Hangzhou. The completion report says the environmental management plans were complied with satisfactorily, that additional environmental assessments were prepared for the components added at restructuring, and that the landfill expansion also produces electricity for about 8,000 households from recovered landfill gas. The Independent Evaluation Group records the Bank's view that the project had positive effects on cultural heritage conservation in Shaoxing.

lvwhy.project: A World Bank loan of US$133 million paid for the wastewater plants, sewers, roads, landfill expansion and heritage works that required the land and the houses.
lvwhy.land: 141.92 hectares were permanently acquired and 161,064 square metres of housing and shop premises demolished across eight sub-projects.

cases.whole: The loan paid for wastewater collection and treatment in Ningbo, the Zhenhai and Jiangnan sewerage works, the clean-up of Dongqian Lake, infrastructure and heritage conservation in the Shaoxing historic city centre and the Yue Kingdom area, the expansion of the Hangzhou Tianziling landfill, and institutional development, with two components added in 2008 and 2009 out of loan savings. The completion report says about 2,290 households, about 20,000 people, benefited from the Shaoxing historic city-centre works, and that households there made their own additional investments in upgrading their housing. The Independent Evaluation Group rated the project's efficiency modest for want of evidence on cost-effectiveness, and notes that a planned transfer of non-operating assets at the old landfill site to the Hangzhou Solid Waste Company was not achieved as designed. All the figures are the Bank's own. No independent check was found.

cases.title: Hubei Yiba expressway: 1,038 families relocated between Yichang and Badong
cases.place: Yichang to Badong expressway corridor, western Hubei, China
cases.point: Approximate. The coordinates sit mid-corridor in the mountains between Yichang and Badong, west of the Three Gorges dam. The expressway runs 173.6 km with 44.1 km of connecting roads through four counties and one municipal district, and the Bank's appraisal expected 53 villages to be affected. This is the 2009-2016 expressway project, not the earlier Three Gorges dam resettlement in the same part of Hubei.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Hubei Yiba Highway Project, P101258. Loan IBRD-76760 of US$150 million, approved 31 March 2009, with the loan agreement conformed on 31 August 2009, effective 21 December 2009, restructured 4 March 2011 and closed 31 December 2015. The whole US$150 million was disbursed. The loan was less than 8 per cent of total project cost.

cases.conditions: The project was Category A for environmental assessment and triggered the Bank's policies on natural habitats, physical cultural resources and involuntary resettlement. A resettlement action plan and a policy framework were prepared in 2008 and disclosed before appraisal, and the Hubei Provincial Communications Department set up a dedicated Hubei Expressway Resettlement Office to run and monitor the resettlement. The Independent Evaluation Group records that the social assessment at appraisal expected the project to affect 9,845 people in 53 villages, with 1,543 households affected by land acquisition and 991 households by demolition of private housing. A complaints system was set up allowing affected people to lodge complaints by internet or text message. Mis-procurement was declared early in implementation and the affected loan amount was used, without cancellation, through the 2011 restructuring.

companies.name: Hubei Provincial Communications Department (HPCD)
companies.role: Implementing agency; set up the Hubei Expressway Resettlement Office (HERO)
companies.desc: The provincial transport authority in Hubei, central China. It ran the expressway works and, through a dedicated resettlement office, the land acquisition and house moves. The completion report says it had run four earlier Bank-financed expressway projects.

companies.name: Hubei Provincial Yiba Expressway Construction Headquarter (HPYECH)
companies.role: Construction body; continues geological investigation and landslide monitoring
companies.desc: The body set up to build the Yichang-Badong expressway. The Independent Evaluation Group records that it continues to investigate the geology and monitor landslides along the road.

cases.community: The completion report says that by project completion 4,325 persons in 1,038 families were relocated, an increase of about 1,000 persons on the resettlement action plan, in order to avoid impacting an environmentally sensitive area. Its own Annex 10, a resettlement case study, gives the same household figure with a different number of people: "Some 1,038 families were relocated, involving 3,736 persons." The report does not explain the difference. About 645 hectares of land were required in four counties and one municipal district, including 205 hectares of cultivated land, and 288,000 square metres of buildings were cleared, including about 92,000 square metres of brick-and-concrete buildings and 196,000 square metres of earth-brick and lower-grade buildings. Eight centralised resettlement sites were designed and built. The report says 35 per cent of the displaced families chose to move to those sites and 65 per cent chose to rebuild near their original house plots, after four rounds of consultation run through the village committees; elsewhere in the same annex the figures appear the other way round, with 35 per cent moved into new sites and 65 per cent relocated in their original villages. The report says the living conditions of displaced families in the project area were lower than in other regions of China and that cultivated land was more limited, and that women as well as men were able to withdraw their compensation. An independent consultant surveyed a random 25 per cent of displaced families in 2014: about 81 per cent said they were satisfied with their living conditions after resettlement, about 80 per cent were satisfied with the compensation, and 69 per cent said their living conditions were better in 2014 than in 2008. The share of families with above-average income was put at 57 per cent against 45 per cent in 2008. No individual village is named in the documents opened.
cases.killed_note: The Independent Evaluation Group records that road accident rates on the existing roads fell from 425 at baseline to 153 at project closure while fatalities on those roads rose from 34 to 35, against a target of reducing them to 18, and says there were no project activities related to that target. Those are road deaths on the existing road network, not deaths caused by the project, and they are not counted here.
cases.outcome: The resettlement is recorded as compliant. The completion report of 21 June 2016 rates the outcome Satisfactory, Bank performance Satisfactory, borrower performance Satisfactory and risk to the development outcome Moderate, with quality of supervision Highly Satisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 9 February 2017 agrees on outcome, Bank performance and borrower performance, recording no disagreement, and rates risk to the development outcome Modest; its ratings table prints Modest in the completion report's column as well, where the completion report's own summary gives Moderate. The Group says resettlement and rehabilitation of project-affected people was deemed satisfactory, and records three incidents of non-compliance with the environmental management plan during implementation, which were rectified by closure. It also cites a Bank case study, "Transformative Potential of World Bank Safeguards Policies: Case Study Series 3 from Yichang-Badong expressway Project in China", which found that by the end of the project most resettled households had better access to roads, electricity and water than before.
cases.displaced_label: families relocated by project completion (World Bank completion report); the report's main text gives 4,325 persons for those families and its own Annex 10 gives 3,736
cases.displaced_note: The World Bank's completion report gives two different numbers of people for the same households. Its main text says that by project completion 4,325 persons in 1,038 families were relocated. Its Annex 10 says 1,038 families were relocated involving 3,736 persons. Both refer to the position at completion and the report does not explain the difference, so the household figure is used here. The Independent Evaluation Group repeats only the 1,038 families. The appraisal social assessment, as reported by the Group, expected the project to affect 9,845 people in 53 villages, with 991 households affected by demolition of private housing. ICIJ puts displacement for this project at 8,380 and lists it in its confirmed-displacement table. No figure in the Bank's documents opened matches 8,380. ICIJ's own method page states what its figures count. It looked for what the Bank's documents call "Project-Affected People (PAP)" or "displaced people", searching those documents for the words "affected", "PAP" or "displaced". Where a document counted only households, it says it was necessary to look up the average number of family members per household. Because the documents do not all separate temporary impacts from permanent ones, it "decided to include all impacts". Its data stops at 31 December 2014. The documents do not explain how ICIJ arrived at its figure.

sources.title: About Evicted and Abandoned: methodology

cases.confidence_note: The core harm rests on one body of evidence. The World Bank's own documents are the only source found: the completion report, written by Bank staff with a borrower section annexed, and the Independent Evaluation Group's validation of that report. Those findings are the lender reporting on its own project. No press report, NGO field study, court record or Inspection Panel complaint about this resettlement was found. Searches in Chinese, including for the project corridor and for named places in it, returned only World Bank documents and local government notices. The satisfaction figures come from a consultant engaged for the project, and the two person-counts for the relocated families appear in the same Bank report without explanation.
cases.ecosystem: The expressway was built on a new alignment through the deeply mountainous Three Gorges area of western Hubei, crossing the Three Gorges National Geological Park, the Shennongjia scenic areas, the Xiaofeng tourism area and karst country whose aquifers supply water. Four cultural relics were identified along the alignment: the Baihuguan ruin, the Pingyikou tombs, the Xinping overhanging coffins and the Niejiahe ancient camp ruins. Expected impacts included solid waste, wastewater, vehicle pollution, dust, soil erosion, noise and loss of patches of natural vegetation. An independent environmental supervisor was empowered to sign contractors' payment certificates, so that only contractors meeting the minimum environmental management requirement were paid. Three incidents of non-compliance with the environmental management plan occurred during implementation and were rectified by closure. Segments of the expressway are in ground prone to landslides, which continued after the road opened to traffic; the construction headquarters continues geological investigation and landslide monitoring, and the Independent Evaluation Group says there is a risk that the benefits may not be sustainable because of the area's vulnerability to natural disasters.

lvwhy.project: A World Bank loan of US$150 million paid for the pavement and traffic facilities over the whole length of the expressway whose construction required the land and the houses.
lvwhy.land: About 645 hectares were required, including 205 hectares of cultivated land, and 288,000 square metres of buildings were cleared.

cases.whole: The loan paid for pavement, traffic facilities and part of the subgrade works on 173.6 km of expressway with 44.1 km of connecting roads between Yichang and Badong, the last and most difficult section of the Shanghai-Chengdu inter-provincial highway. Over 74 per cent of the expressway consists of tunnels and bridges, with 148 bridges totalling 70 km, and the cost was about US$13.4 million per kilometre. The road opened in stages, the last section to traffic on 27 December 2014. Travel time on the expressway at closure was 2.17 hours against five hours on the existing roads. Project costs at completion exceeded appraisal costs by 29 per cent, largely because of unexpected landslides that required a substantial volume of added landslide treatment works. All the figures are the Bank's own. No independent check was found.

cases.title: Vietnam road asset project: 105 households moved, and land clearance on Highway 9 left unfinished
cases.place: National highways 2, 6, 38 and 9 and the Son La city bypass, Viet Nam; coordinates on the Son La bypass
cases.point: Approximate. The coordinates sit on Son La city, where the project built a bypass and where the largest documented land clearance took place. The project covered national highways in several provinces, including National Highway 38 in the north, National Highway 2, National Highway 6 through Hoa Binh and Son La, and National Highway 9 in Quang Tri.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Viet Nam Road Asset Management Project, P123961. Credit IDA-53310 of US$250 million, later revised to US$229.77 million, with trust fund TF-15733 of US$1.29 million. Approved 12 December 2013, effective 14 January 2014, restructured 28 December 2020, closing extended from 31 December 2020 to 31 December 2022. US$205.43 million of the credit was disbursed. The US$50 million of borrower financing planned was revised to zero.

cases.conditions: The project was Category B and triggered the Bank's policies on environmental assessment, natural habitats and involuntary resettlement. A resettlement policy framework was disclosed on 2 August 2013 and resettlement action plans for the original sub-projects in July and August 2013. At the restructuring of December 2020 the policy on indigenous peoples was also triggered, because new road sections on National Highways 2 and 6 crossed areas with ethnic minority populations, and Ethnic Minority Development Plans were required. A supplementary resettlement action plan for the National Highway 9 sub-project was approved by the Quang Tri provincial people's committee and disclosed on 10 January 2022, before land acquisition began there.

companies.name: Directorate for Roads of Viet Nam (DRVN), Project Management Unit 3
companies.role: Implementing agency for the works, land acquisition and resettlement
companies.desc: The national roads authority under Vietnam's transport ministry, and the project management unit that ran this credit. The Bank's completion report says it addressed the outstanding items of the post-closing action plan by August 2022.

companies.name: Quang Tri Provincial People's Committee
companies.role: Responsible for land clearance on the National Highway 9 sub-project
companies.hq: Dong Ha, Quang Tri, Viet Nam
companies.desc: The provincial government in central Vietnam. Vietnam's Government Inspectorate concluded in 2025 that it had not carried out land clearance as committed on the National Highway 9 upgrade.

cases.community: The completion report says the number of affected households at the end of the project, after careful road realignment, was 4,672, of which 105 project-affected households were relocated. It says compensation for all affected households for resettlement and land acquisition under the original activities was completed, including those under the additional activities, and that of 6,661 affected households that were direct beneficiaries for compensation, 87.09 per cent were female-headed. It says complaints through the grievance system were mainly about the adequacy of compensation payments and that all were resolved by closing. Social safeguards performance at the end of the project was rated Moderately Unsatisfactory because of resettlement still pending under the post-closing action plan. The scope of work on National Highway 9, the 13.8 km section from Cua Viet port to National Highway 1 in Quang Tri, was cancelled by project closing because of delayed land acquisition and resettlement, and construction there stopped on 31 December 2022, leaving outstanding environmental problems that the report lists as traffic safety, site restoration, water supply continuity, blockages of two small local irrigation canals and limitation of river flow by a bridge. An annexed account quoting Son La city officials describes the clearance for the bypass: the 15 km section through Son La city affected 589 households and recovered 51.48 hectares in the communes and wards of Chieng Co, Hua La, Chieng Coi and Chieng Sinh, with 81 land recovery decisions issued since 2018 covering over 57.44 hectares from 589 households and compensation of more than VND 136 billion. For the bypass as a whole the account gives 70.3 hectares recovered from 803 households.
cases.outcome: The completion report of 29 September 2023 rates the project outcome Satisfactory and Bank performance Satisfactory, and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 12 March 2024 agrees, recording no disagreement. Within that, the completion report rates social safeguards performance at the end of the project Moderately Unsatisfactory, because of resettlement still pending under the post-closing action plan, and environmental safeguards Moderately Unsatisfactory, because of the outstanding problems on National Highway 9. The Independent Evaluation Group's own safeguards section does not carry those two ratings: it says that according to the completion report the project complied with the environmental safeguard policies and that safeguards compliance during implementation was rated Satisfactory or Moderately Satisfactory, citing page 24 of the report, the page on which the Moderately Unsatisfactory ratings appear. The Group notes inconsistencies in the slow release of counterpart funds for land acquisition, and says Bank money was used for activities with fewer encumbrances while waiting for the government to release funds. Separately, Vietnam's Government Inspectorate issued conclusion 375/KL-TTCP on 14 October 2025 on the National Highway 9 upgrade, a project financed by this World Bank loan. As reported by the state newspaper Bao Thanh tra on 18 November 2025, the inspectorate found that compensation, support, resettlement and land clearance had been split off into a separate sub-project and left out of the investment totals approved for appraisal, which it held to breach several laws and decrees; that some land clearance sites were cleared late and some not at all, so contractors could not get access; and that a main cause was that the Quang Tri provincial people's committee did not carry out land clearance as committed. It records that the loan agreement was not extended and the project has been stopped since 31 December 2022, that annual capital allocations were cut by VND 50,000 million in 2022 and VND 48,909 million in 2023, and it recommends disciplinary accountability for leaders at the construction ministry, the finance ministry and Quang Tri province. The article does not give the number of households affected on that section.
cases.displaced_label: project-affected households relocated, out of 4,672 affected households at the end of the project (World Bank completion report)
cases.displaced_note: The World Bank's completion report counts 4,672 affected households at the end of the project and says 105 of them were relocated. It gives no number of people. A separate account annexed to the report, quoting Son La city officials, says land was recovered from 589 households for the 15 km section of the bypass through Son La city and from 803 households for the bypass as a whole; that is land recovery, not relocation. ICIJ puts displacement for this project at 7,788 and lists it in its confirmed-displacement table. No figure in the Bank's documents opened matches 7,788. ICIJ's own method page states what its figures count. It looked for what the Bank's documents call "Project-Affected People (PAP)" or "displaced people", searching those documents for the words "affected", "PAP" or "displaced". Where a document counted only households, it says it was necessary to look up the average number of family members per household. Because the documents do not all separate temporary impacts from permanent ones, it "decided to include all impacts". Its data stops at 31 December 2014. The documents do not explain how ICIJ arrived at its figure.

cases.confidence_note: The counts of affected and relocated households, and the Moderately Unsatisfactory safeguards ratings, come from the World Bank's own completion report, which is the lender reporting on its own project. The failure of land clearance on National Highway 9 is also recorded outside the Bank, by Vietnam's Government Inspectorate in conclusion 375/KL-TTCP of 14 October 2025, as reported by the state newspaper Bao Thanh tra; the inspectorate's own text was not opened here, so its findings are given as that newspaper reports them. The World Bank's Independent Evaluation Group describes the completion report's safeguards ratings differently from the report itself, and both versions are set out above rather than reconciled.
cases.ecosystem: The project triggered the Bank's natural habitats policy. The completion report says environmental management plans were prepared and written into bidding documents, that compliance problems were identified over enforcement of the environmental and social management plan and over traffic safety and occupational health and safety, and that these were mitigated. At closing it rates environmental safeguards Moderately Unsatisfactory because of outstanding problems on the National Highway 9 section where construction stopped on 31 December 2022: traffic safety, site restoration, water supply continuity, blockages of two small local irrigation canals, and limitation of river flow by the construction of a bridge.

lvwhy.project: A World Bank credit of US$250 million, revised to US$229.77 million, paid for the road upgrading and maintenance works that required the land.
lvwhy.land: 4,672 households were affected by land acquisition, 105 of them relocated, and in Son La city alone 81 land recovery decisions took over 57.44 hectares from 589 households.

cases.whole: The credit paid for upgrading and periodic maintenance of national highways, performance-based maintenance contracts and a road asset management system for the Directorate for Roads of Viet Nam. About 80.53 km of road had been upgraded by 31 December 2022, including sections of National Highway 38, 19.5 km of National Highway 6 and the Son La city bypass, built from project savings. The share of roads in good and fair condition reached 72.32 per cent against a target of 72 per cent. The National Highway 9 expansion in Quang Tri, also financed from project savings, was cancelled by closing; the government said it would finish the work with its own money, expected in 2024, and Vietnam's Government Inspectorate recorded in October 2025 that the project had been stopped since the end of 2022 and asked the province to seek funds to restart it.

dropped.candidate: China: Fujian Meizhou Bay Navigation Improvement Project (P124848)
dropped.reason: No one was physically displaced, so there is nothing to map as displacement. The Bank's completion report of 20 December 2019 was downloaded and read in full from disk: it says the Bank-financed project caused no physical resettlement to local households, that the project and linked activities affected the livelihoods of 98 households comprising 506 persons and that no household relocation was required, and elsewhere that land reclaimed by the government affected 5,006 persons in 986 households and that in total the project affected the livelihood of 5,016 persons from 987 households, without household relocation. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 12 June 2020 was also read. ICIJ puts displacement at 9,255; the documents count nobody moved. Opened: the completion report, the Evaluation Group review, and the project's document list in the Bank's documents API (appraisal document, loan agreement for Loan 8227-CN, two resettlement plans of 2012, restructuring paper of 2018).

No document counts anyone actually relocated. The Bank's completion report of 23 April 2018 was downloaded and read from disk. Its only household figure is an appraisal estimate: resettlement "would take place in 17 villages and would impact 376 households (1,570 people), who were resettled under the client-financed Component 3". The borrower's section of the same report gives the outcome in area rather than people: 959 mu of permanent land acquired and 22,200.6 square metres of houses and structures demolished for the main project, about 940 mu and 41,724 square metres less than planned, plus 224.38 mu and 6,336 square metres under the additional financing, with compensation of RMB 132.74 million and RMB 58.69 million. Since the demolition came in far below plan, the appraisal estimate of 376 households cannot be treated as an outcome. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 24 September 2018 was read in full and carries no resettlement figures. ICIJ puts displacement at 8,881, which matches nothing in the documents. Opened: the completion report, the Evaluation Group review, and the project's document list (appraisal document, loan agreements for Loans 7692-CN and 7937-CN, resettlement plans of 2007 and 2015).

dropped.candidate: CN-Jiangxi Poyang Lake Basin and Ecological Economic Zone Small Town Development Project (P126856)
dropped.reason: The outcome figure counts people affected, not people moved, and no document counts the households relocated. The Bank's completion report of 27 June 2020 was downloaded and read from disk: it says the project affected a total of 10,873 people including land acquisition and relocation, that the final resettlement impact was higher than expected at appraisal because newly added urban transport sub-projects brought additional resettlement, that all compensation due was fully disbursed, and that all the relocated households had moved into replacement houses, 53 per cent choosing replacement houses, 44 per cent self-construction on government-provided land and 3 per cent cash. It gives no number of relocated households. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 16 February 2021 gives only the appraisal plan: about 7,200 people in over 1,600 households expected to be affected by land acquisition, and house demolition expected to relocate 900 people from 230 households. ICIJ puts displacement at 8,477. A World Bank Integrity Vice Presidency redacted report of March 2019 on this project was also read; it concerns a bidder, Company A, that misrepresented the values of two prior contracts in its bids for two project contracts and was debarred with conditional release, and the contracts were not awarded to it. That is a procurement finding, not a resettlement one. Opened: the completion report, the Evaluation Group review, the integrity report, and the project's document list (appraisal document, loan agreement for Loan 8234-CN and its 2018 amendment, resettlement plan of 2012, restructuring paper of 2018).

The loan was cancelled before any works money was spent, and no document counts anyone relocated. There is no completion report; the Bank published a Note on Cancelled Operation on 4 December 2014, which was downloaded and read in full from disk. It records Loan 7929-CN of US$150 million, approved 10 June 2010, signed November 2010, effective 12 January 2011, and says that after more than three years no contracts had been awarded and nothing was disbursed from the loan except the front-end fee of US$375,000, after which the borrower proposed to cancel the project and prepay. It records a safeguards failure: resettlement for Taihang Road began in March 2013, and on 31 December 2013 the independent external resettlement monitoring agency reported to the Bank that Taiyuan Municipality "did not adequately compensate for land belonging to state-own enterprises and institutes, and thus was not in compliance with the project Resettlement Action Plan". That non-compliance concerns land held by state-owned enterprises and institutes, not households, and the note counts no household or person moved anywhere in its 760 lines of text. Inadequate counterpart funding had suspended land acquisition and resettlement on Taihang Road, and resettlement costs rose after a change in government policy on resettlement and compensation in 2011. ICIJ puts displacement at 7,752. With no relocation count, no disbursement to the works and the resettlement carried out with domestic funds, there is no harm here that can be tied to the loan at a documented scale. Opened: the Note on Cancelled Operation, the project record in the Bank's projects API, and the project's document list (appraisal document, loan agreement for Loan 7929-CN, resettlement policy framework and resettlement action plan of 2008, five implementation status reports).
